old_row.relationship: Same-chapter specified boundary segment within Zebulun's allocation
old_row.rationale: Gola, the sea-side Maragella boundary and the ravine facing Jekman belong to the border account closed as Zebulun's city-and-village inheritance.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter specified boundary segment within Zebulun's allocation
new_row.rationale: Gola, the sea and Maragella borders, and the ravine facing Jekman belong to the account closed as Zebulun's city-and-village inheritance, without assigning Maragella a modern coastal identity.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter named hill-country city group and tribal closure
old_row.rationale: Armaith, Arael and Hazor occur within the city sequence closed as Naphtali's inheritance, without identifying them with similarly named towns in other allotments.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter named city group and tribal closure
new_row.rationale: Armaith, Arael and Hazor occur within the city sequence closed as Naphtali's inheritance, without identifying them with similarly named towns in other allotments.

old_row.relationship: Levitical petition cites the town-and-pasture command
old_row.rationale: The Levites request dwelling cities and surrounding lands for cattle through Moses' command; Numbers expressly directs Israel to supply towns and livestock lands from their possessions.

new_row.relationship: Levitical petition cites the town-and-pasture command
new_row.rationale: The Levites request dwelling cities and surrounding lands for livestock through Moses' command; Numbers expressly directs Israel to supply towns and livestock lands from their possessions.

old_row.relationship: Different campaigns sharing spoil beyond the fighting group
old_row.rationale: Both describe sharing enemy spoil with the wider brothers or congregation; Numbers explicitly divides between warriors and the congregation, without specifying Joshua's later distribution proportions.

new_row.relationship: Related enemy-spoil distributions with distinct recipient descriptions
new_row.rationale: Both describe enemy spoil being shared; Numbers specifies warriors and the whole congregation, while Joshua says the eastern tribes divided it with their brothers and gives no distribution proportions.

old_row.relationship: Achar's devoted-property offense and collective losses
old_row.rationale: The recital connects Achar's offense with communal wrath and deaths; Joshua7 names the Zerah-line ancestry more fully and narrates Israel's defeat with about thirty-six killed.

new_row.relationship: Achar's devoted-property offense and collective losses
new_row.rationale: Both link Achar's devoted-property offense with communal wrath; Joshua7 narrates about thirty-six killed and gives Carmi and Zambri between Achar and Zerah, preserving the differing ancestry formulations.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter no-offense verdict after the stated testimonial defense
old_row.rationale: Phinehas' favorable verdict follows the explicit non-sacrificial testimony explanation and denial of an altar apart from the Lord's tent, without turning the initial allegation into a finding.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter no-offense verdict after the stated testimonial defense
new_row.rationale: Phinehas' favorable verdict follows the explicit non-sacrificial testimony explanation and rejection of offering apart from the Lord's altar before His tent, without turning the initial allegation into a finding.

old_row.relationship: One pursuing a thousand under different descriptions of divine agency
old_row.rationale: Both use one pursuing a thousand; Joshua credits the Lord fighting for Israel, whereas Deuteronomy asks how such pursuit occurs unless God sells and hands over those pursued.

new_row.relationship: One pursuing a thousand under different descriptions of divine agency
new_row.rationale: Both use one pursuing a thousand; Joshua credits the Lord fighting for Israel, whereas Deuteronomy's rhetorical question uses God's selling and handing-over language without assigning its pronouns a new referent.

old_row.relationship: Divine refusal of destruction and curse reversed into blessing
old_row.rationale: Both describe the Lord preserving Israel and blessing despite Balaam's intended curse; Deuteronomy expressly says He refused Balaam and changed the curse because of His love.

new_row.relationship: Divine refusal of destruction and curse reversed into blessing
new_row.rationale: Both describe the Lord preserving Israel and blessing despite the curse sought through Balaam; Deuteronomy expressly says He refused Balaam and changed the curse because of His love.

old_row.relationship: Other-god service followed by delivery to enemies
old_row.rationale: Both connect service to Astarte-related gods with the Lord handing Israel to enemies; Joshua's continuation specifically names Moab's Eglom, while Judges2 gives the broader pattern.

new_row.relationship: Other-god service followed by delivery to enemies
new_row.rationale: Both connect serving other gods with the Lord handing Israel to enemies; Joshua names Astarte, Ashtaroth and Eglom, while Judges names Baal and Astartes with a broader enemy description.
